7. **Edit a file** → `ccx code edit <file> --at A-B#hash --content <text>` (hash-verified write: refuses on anchor mismatch, re-anchors moved content, returns the new anchor so edits chain; `--content -` reads stdin, `--delete` removes the range; `--match <text>` addresses by exact bytes instead of a span — an ambiguous match errors listing candidate anchors, `--at` scopes the scan, `--all` replaces every occurrence)
8. **Review changes** → `ccx vcs diff [src]` (structural, jj-aware; exact hunks: `git diff -- <file>`)
9. **Inspect one commit** → `ccx vcs show [ref]` (message + structural per-file diff; default `@-`/HEAD)
10. **How a file evolved** → `ccx vcs history <path> [-n N]` (per-commit sha · date · subject + changed symbols)
11. **Locate a repo/module/package on disk** → `ccx repo locate <name>` (sibling repo, Go module, or Python package by import or dist name; prints tab-separated `kind`/`path`/`version` rows — an installed Python package yields both its sibling `repo` row and its installed `package` row; exit 3 when nothing resolves)
12. **Read installed dependency source** (`.venv`, site-packages, vendored) → spawn the `cc-context:dep-reader` agent with the package and your question — cited conclusions come back, the source never enters your context. Inline: `ccx repo locate <pkg>` for the on-disk path, then entries 4/6 with that path (`-g <path>` or an anchored glob) — never raw `rg` into `.venv`
13. **Commit, push, watch CI** → `ccx vcs ship -m "<msg>" [paths...]` (jj-aware commit + push + a watch over every workflow run on the pushed commit, in one call — per-run `workflow · conclusion · duration · url` report, plus failing jobs and a `--budget`-capped log excerpt when a run goes red; trailing paths scope the commit to just those files, leaving the rest of a shared working copy untouched; scoping goes below the file too — `ccx vcs hunks [paths...]` lists every pending hunk as a stable `file:A-B#hash` ref, and repeatable `--skip-hunk <ref>`/`--only-hunk <ref>` commit a file partially without ever rewriting it on disk, leaving excluded hunks (a concurrent session's, say) uncommitted in `@`, and refusing outright when a selection would cut an empty commit or a ref has drifted; an empty working copy refuses outright too (`nothing to commit` — a prior ship likely already landed it) instead of cutting an empty duplicate; and where the commit goes is one decision, resolved before any mutation and reported as a `branch <name>` or `created <name>` segment — on a non-trunk branch or bookmark ship appends to it, on trunk it appends in your own repositories and starts a branch when GitHub positively says the repository is someone else's (an org trunk rejects the commit through its protect hook and leaves it dangling; the native GitHub stack lane and the legacy gt lane always branch on trunk; actual native membership takes precedence, existing Graphite membership stays on Graphite until migrated, `ccx.stack` (`github|graphite`) selects the backend for new or untracked stacks, `--no-stack` bypasses both stack lanes, and `--no-gt` bypasses the legacy Graphite lane only while leaving native GitHub stacks active; plain git and jj ship outside both stack lanes open ordinary PRs, whereas the native stack lane also registers actual native stack metadata and edits exactly the fields this invocation restated; raw `gt` commands, hooks, and rules apply only to the legacy gt backend, while the native lane uses the GitHub stack API, local catalog, and git operations under the same ccx safety checks; ccx derives the name from the commit subject itself, slugified and capped, keeping the `Claude-Session-Id` trailer out of it), a detached HEAD or an ambiguous trunk refuses, and `--branch <name>`, `--new-branch[=<name>]`, `--append`, and `--allow-trunk` state intent explicitly (`--bookmark` is the jj-only alias of `--branch`, `--create` the deprecated alias of `--new-branch`; `--new-branch name` and `--new-branch=name` both name the branch, `--` keeps the positionals after a bare `--new-branch` as paths, and a name that is also a path on disk is refused as ambiguous); an updated remote is handled in-call on both backends — ship fetches first and rebases the stack onto the target (jj bookmark, or `origin/<branch>` on plain git, autostashing uncommitted work), rolling back and reporting a rebase that would conflict, and a push that still loses the race to a concurrent push re-fetches, re-rebases, and retries up to 3 attempts before failing with the manual recovery steps — though a rejected `--amend` push refuses instead of force-retrying over the other session's work). A live Graphite config (`.git/.graphite_repo_config`, resolved through the git common dir so a linked worktree counts) makes the gt lane a candidate — even in colocated jj repos; `--no-gt` falls back to the jj>git detection, and three gates run before any mutation, each demoting to the jj/git lane with the reason named in a leading `lane <kind> (<reason>)` segment: `ccx.nogt` set in git config (the durable opt-out for a repo carrying a stale Graphite config), GitHub positively saying the repo is someone else's — public, and you neither administer it nor share an owner or organization with it (a lookup that cannot be made keeps the lane) — and a cached probe of whether Graphite can actually submit here, since the config alone only proves `gt init` once ran (a probe that times out or cannot reach Graphite demotes too — a lane nobody could confirm is not one to ride — and each verdict caches for its own span: a yes a day, a no an hour, an unanswered probe a minute, so an outage costs one probe a minute, not one per command). On the gt lane commits go through gt (`gt create <name>` starts a stacked branch, `gt modify -c` appends to one, `--amend` amends the branch tip; an untracked branch is adopted first with `gt track -f`, `--parent` naming its parent — refused before any commit forms when the resolved parent is a branch the remote trunk already contains, pointing at `--parent <branch>` and `ccx vcs prune` instead), and the push no longer shells to `gt submit` at all: the gt lane calls Graphite's HTTP API directly (`internal/gtapi`), force-pushing every branch of the downstack in one atomic multi-ref push and then posting one submit entry per branch, bottom-up — published by default, `--draft` opts out, `--publish` says so explicitly — and since none of it runs through `gt` itself, none of it shows up in gt's own debug logs. The submit anchors on the remote trunk rather than the local one, fetching exactly one ref (`origin/<trunk>`, moving no local branch and no working copy) and reading each branch's base sha and each new pull request's title and body range off it — a local trunk left behind the remote used to make an already-upstream branch look like a real stack member, and Graphite refused the empty pull request that followed; past that one ref ship still never fetches, and it never retries there. Every downstack branch whose head the remote trunk already contains is dropped from the push and named as skipped, and ship refuses outright when the branch being shipped is itself already contained, pointing at `ccx vcs prune` — which now reparents the graphite rows it forgets onto the first surviving ancestor with trunk as the floor and strikes each forgotten row from its parent's children, so a prune cannot strand a stack in either direction. A `needs_restack` anywhere on the downstack, or a base off the fetched trunk, is no longer a refusal: ship commits first and then runs the stack rebase over the downstack, reported as `restacked in isolation`; the working copy holding a moved branch must be clean, and a conflict stops in a `conflict-<branch>` workspace with rerere off, where `ccx vcs stack continue` finishes the rebase, pushes, submits, and restates the PR flags, and `ccx vcs stack abort` drops the run; ship still refuses up front on a branch gt cannot adopt, or on `--amend` on trunk, and a failed submit reports its recovery step instead of retrying (`gt auth` for a rejected token; a push refused past its lease reports the git error, and `ccx vcs stack submit` restacks and resubmits the stack), the report reading `submitted <branch> → PR #<n> <url>`. Ship owns the pull request in every lane: `--pr-title`/`--pr-body-file` are repeatable and branch-scoped (`<branch>=<value>`, a bare value applying to the tip; `--pr-body-file -` reads stdin once, and every body file is read before the commit forms) — outside the gt lane ship opens the branch's PR when there is none and edits exactly the fields this invocation restated when there is, so a hand-edited description survives a re-ship that does not mention it; in the gt lane it fills the title and body `gt submit` leaves empty, the only way a downstack PR gets a body at all; `--draft`/`--publish` apply in every lane, converting an existing PR in either direction, `--no-pr` opts out, and a ship naming no PR flag makes no `gh pr` call. `--reviews` chains a review watch (entry 14) after the CI watch. A red run hands off to the `cc-context:ci-triage` agent — spawn it with the run id for root cause, a minimal excerpt, and the next step instead of the full log
14. **Stream PR review comments** → `ccx vcs reviews [pr-or-branch...]` (attaches to open PRs — positionals mix PR numbers and branch names, none → the current branch's PR, `--stack` → the selected native GitHub or legacy Graphite downstack — and polls every `--interval` (default 30s), streaming each review verdict, inline comment, and issue comment as one block with author, locus, and a `--budget`-capped body; a `changes_requested` review carries a pointer to spawn the `cc-context:pr-review-triage` agent with the PR and review id; the watch exits when every watched PR is merged or closed, and Ctrl-C prints the exact resume command; `--since` replays history — RFC3339, a duration ago like `90m`, or `all`, default now — so arm a `Monitor` on `ccx vcs reviews --since 5m` right after a ship to close the gap between push and attach; the watch is at-least-once, so a resume may re-print events already seen; `ship --reviews` chains the same watch in-call after CI)
15. **Bring the stack current with trunk** → `ccx vcs stack restack` (lane-selected like ship, gates included — the native GitHub and legacy gt stack lanes run `ccx vcs stack rebase --no-push`, jj fetches and rebases the working-copy stack onto `trunk()` and rolls a conflict back, plain git replays the branch onto the fetched remote default branch; on the stack and git lanes a conflict moves nothing and stops in a `conflict-<branch>` workspace with rerere off, where `ccx vcs stack continue` finishes the rebase once the files are resolved and added and `ccx vcs stack abort` drops the run — never headless resolution; `--no-stack` forces the jj/git lane, while `--no-gt` bypasses only the legacy gt lane). `ccx vcs stack rebase` rebases the whole stack onto trunk and pushes it; the working copy holding a moved branch must be clean. The rest of the group cuts and lands such a stack — `ccx vcs stack new <name>` cuts a branch stacked on this one **in a working copy of its own**, leaving the calling one on its branch, `ccx vcs stack list` names the working copy holding each branch, and `ccx vcs stack submit` restacks every lane and then submits the whole stack
16. **Compose several calls / post-process any output** → `ccx exec '<python>'` — a sandboxed script whose async host functions are every ccx query op, a gated `sh(cmd)`, and every stateless MCP server's tools (auto-reflected, no flag needed); only the script's return value enters context. Rule of thumb: one question → one ccx call (entries 1–15, 17–23); a pipeline, filter, fan-out, or any output you'd immediately post-process (project a JSON blob, sweep signatures across files, join search hits) → exec. Discover the host functions and the Python-subset rules with `ccx exec --list-tools` (MCP: `ccx_exec_tools`), once per session.
17. **Re-encode JSON tool output** → `ccx format -- <cmd>` (or `… | ccx format`) — a shape classifier picks the leanest encoding (prose, markdown table, CSV/TSV, TOON, TRON, JSONL, or compact JSON), never larger than compact JSON by bytes; `--format=X` forces one encoder
18. **Map a web page** → `ccx web outline <url>` (heading tree with stable `§` section refs; pages cache 24h, `--refresh` refetches)
19. **Read one section of a page** → `ccx web read <url> --section <ref>` (budget-capped section subtree + prev/next nav; whole page: `--full`)
20. **Ask a question of a page** → `ccx web search <url> "<question>"` (top-k relevant chunks with `<url> §2.3#hash` cites; hybrid BM25 + local embeddings — native in-process, no `uv`; BM25-only with a note when the model weights are unavailable, i.e. offline with an empty cache)
21. **Which lane a mutating vcs command takes, and why** → `ccx vcs info` (alias `lane`; vcs kind, selected stack and queue providers — native GitHub stacks in `<git-common-dir>/gh-stack` at schema version 1 vs Graphite, with actual native branch membership taking precedence, existing Graphite membership kept until migrated, `ccx.stack` (`github|graphite`) choosing new or untracked stacks, `--no-stack` bypassing both, `--no-gt` retained for legacy compatibility, and `ccx.queue` (`trunk` with `TRUNK_MERGE_API_KEY`) selecting the queue provider — plus repo root, branch, trunk, dirty state, Graphite config/CLI/reachability, the GitHub repo record, and the downstack with each branch's PR and whether that PR has a body; `--json`, `--refresh` refetches the cached GitHub metadata and reachability verdict, `--no-stack`, `--no-gt`; fails soft when GitHub is unreachable)
22. **A repo's stated contribution rules** → `ccx vcs guidelines` (alias `contributing`; every PR template variant, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, code of conduct, and issue config, each served verbatim, never summarized — so a PR template can be reproduced down to its checkboxes; the GitHub payload caches for a day but local files re-read every run, since a branch switch changes `CONTRIBUTING.md` on disk; `--json`, `--refresh`, `--full` adds issue-template bodies, `--budget` caps per document)
23. **Every branch of the stack, and what blocks each from landing** → `ccx vcs status` (one batched round trip for the whole stack — per branch, in stack order: its divergence from trunk, whether it sits off its parent in the native GitHub stack API or legacy `gt` state, its pull request's mergeability, the checks on the head and which of them the base branch's protection rule requires, every standing review and whether it was cast on the head, and a `blocked` line per hold. `mergeable` is re-asked once when GitHub answers `UNKNOWN`, which it usually does on a first ask, and CI is read through `statusCheckRollup`, never `gh run list`, so a repository on Buildkite reports its pipeline rather than "no CI". It also reports queue state from the configured queue provider — Trunk via `ccx.queue=trunk` (where an API error stays `UNKNOWN` with no legacy fallback), generic GitHub, or the legacy Graphite merge queue (reconstructing the admitted snapshot from merge labels, draft queue PRs, and the queue's activity comment against the branch's head history); `--json`, `--refresh`, `--no-stack`, `--no-gt`, `--budget` caps the human report)

Entries 9–15 and 21–23 are CLI-only (entry 12's `locate` step included) — the MCP mirrors the query surface (1–8) plus exec (16), format (17, as `BashFormat`), and web (18–20, as `ccx_web_outline`/`ccx_web_read`/`ccx_web_search`), not these.

A path operand missing its extension resolves itself across the path-taking ops: `pkg/events` where only `pkg/events.py` exists runs against the sibling and notes the substitution (`# note: pkg/events → pkg/events.py`); several candidates error listing them, none errors clean (exit 3) — never raw engine stderr.

A one-shot question about a page → spawn the `cc-context:web-fetch` agent with the URL and your prompt verbatim (the WebFetch drop-in: cited answer out, the page never enters your context); research spanning several pages → `cc-context:web-researcher`.

Durable prose — plans, reviews, memory files — cites code as `path:line#hash` (e.g. `internal/render/finalize.go:31#k2fa`); any later session resolves the cite statelessly with ccx, because the hash re-anchors by content even after the file drifts.

Reach for your **LSP** when the answer must be exhaustive/structural (findReferences, rename, goToImplementation) — and verify any complete-set answer ("every subclass", "every importer") by reading the candidate files: bounded views optimize for precision, not exhaustiveness — or spawn the `cc-context:enumerator` agent, which packages that gather-and-verify loop and returns the verified set with cites and named blind spots. Use **Grep/Glob** or `rg` only for literal content in non-source files (logs, JSON, YAML) — on source, raw `rg` is gated the same as raw `grep`.

## Go Style

Target Go 1.26+. Run `task build`, `task test` (`go test -race`), and `task lint`.

**Comments are terse and used sparingly — the code documents itself** through names, types, and organization. The one exception is documentation-generation comments: godoc on exported types, funcs, and the package, each starting with the identifier's name (`// NewRootCmd builds …`); unexported helpers get none. Beyond godoc, comment only for TODOs, non-obvious workarounds, or disabled code — never to restate the signature.

**Errors wrap with `%w`.** Return failures up the stack with `fmt.Errorf("…: %w", err)` and inspect them with `errors.Is` / `errors.As`, never string matching. See STYLEGUIDE.md § Error Handling.

**Structured logging via `log/slog`.** Diagnostics go through the configured default logger (`slog.Info`, `slog.Debug`) with key-value attrs — never `fmt.Println` for logging. See `internal/log`.

@STYLEGUIDE.md

## General Rules

**Minimal changes.** Stay within scope; fix the issue, then stop.

**Match surrounding code.** Follow the conventions of the file you're in, then the package.

**No defensive coding.** No fallbacks, shims, or backwards-compat layers; no guards against impossible states. If unused, delete it. Crash on the unexpected.

**Search before writing.** Before creating a helper, query the codebase via `ccx code search` (intent or symbol queries both work). Sibling packages win over re-implementation.

**Code stewardship.** When you touch a file, fix nearby bugs, style violations, and broken tests; don't wave them off as pre-existing or out of scope.

**Observe, don't infer.** Inspect actual data — read fixtures, dump structs, run the code — before reasoning from assumption.

**Don't use external failures as an excuse to stop.** API quota, rate-limit, and outage errors rarely block the whole task; trace the catch sites and confirm a failure actually stops you before claiming it does.

**Verify before asserting.** Don't report something as working, fixed, blocked, or impossible until you've checked — run it, read the output, reproduce the failure. "It should work" is not "it works."

**Reproduce before fixing.** When something breaks, isolate the smallest failing case before editing or re-running. Re-running the whole command while changing code between runs hides the root cause; narrow to the one failing test or input first.

**Research after repeated failure.** After ~2 failed approaches, stop guessing and gather evidence — search the web, read the docs and source — before a third attempt.

**Get a second opinion on a plateau.** On a debugging plateau (2 failed attempts before a 3rd), a non-trivial architectural decision, or algorithmic/security-sensitive code, get an outside check (e.g. `/codex`) before committing to the approach.

**Don't contort code to satisfy a linter.** The compiler and `golangci-lint` serve the code, not the other way around. Don't widen a type to `any`, bolt on a needless type assertion, or sprinkle `//nolint` just to silence a diagnostic. If a clean fix isn't obvious, leave the diagnostic — a visible one is preferable to scar tissue.

**Mechanical linting.** Running `gofumpt`/`golangci-lint` by hand is fine, and encouraged — the pre-commit hooks (prek: gofumpt + goimports + golangci-lint) also format and lint on every `git commit`; run `uvx prek install` once to activate them. Fix what needs human judgment and let the tooling own the mechanical churn. When reviewing code, don't flag mechanical lint violations (gofmt, import order, line length).

**Testing.** Tests live beside the code as `*_test.go`; run them with `task test` (`go test -race ./...`). Write table-driven tests with strict assertions against specific values, mock the boundaries your code talks to (network, filesystem, clock), and leave the code under test real.

**Writing docs.** When writing or revising docs, a README, a tutorial, a how-to, or reference, use the `writing-docs` skill (Diataxis modes, voice rules, and runnable code-sample rules) and run `slop-cop check <file> --lang=markdown` before you finish (slop-cop is a Go binary; if it's not on PATH, run the `/slop-cop-check` skill — never `uvx slop-cop`).

## Python Style

The Python code under `plugin/` follows `plugin/STYLEGUIDE.md` (Python 3.13+); the primary language follows the root `STYLEGUIDE.md`.

## Hook Style

This repo's capt-hook hooks under `.claude/hooks/` follow `.claude/hooks/STYLEGUIDE.md` (Python 3.13+): never a wrong fire, one concern per hook file, and inline `tests={}` on every registration.

**Version control.** This repo is a colocated `jj` repo over git — prefer `jj` (`jj describe` / `jj commit`, `jj git push`) over raw `git` for day-to-day work. Commits stay atomic and scoped: one logical change each. For the routine commit, push, and watch-CI cycle, `ccx vcs ship -m "<msg>"` runs the whole dance in one call — a jj-aware commit, the push, and a watch over every workflow run on the pushed commit, with a per-run report and failure logs — instead of the three-to-six Bash calls by hand. A working copy shared with a concurrent session is no reason to bypass ship: `ccx vcs ship -m "<msg>" <paths...>` commits only your paths and leaves the rest of `@` untouched. A single file mixing your hunks with a concurrent session's is no reason either: `ccx vcs hunks <file>` lists each pending hunk as a `file:A-B#hash` ref, and `ccx vcs ship --skip-hunk <ref>` commits around the foreign one — the partial commit is cut through jj's diff-editor protocol (git: a temp index), never by rewriting the file on disk. Ship also runs the repo's prek commit hooks (`uvx prek`) before committing. Auto-fixes are folded into the commit and a finding is reported without stopping it, because CI grades the result. A golangci-lint hook that gave no verdict (another run held its lock, a timeout, a load failure) stops the ship with nothing committed, and `--no-verify` skips the gate. Hunk-scoped ships skip it too and report a `hooks hunk-skip` segment, since a partial selection can't be verified externally. The hooks run once per ship: a commit ship has already hooked itself carries `--no-verify`, so git's `pre-commit` hook doesn't re-run them through prek's unstaged-stash path, which restores from the current index rather than a pinned tree and reports a failed restore only on stderr. A repo ship didn't hook keeps its own git hooks — no prek config, no `uvx`, a jj repo with no `.git`, a hunk selection, or a config declaring a `commit-msg`/`prepare-commit-msg` stage that `prek run --files` never reaches. Where the commit goes resolves before the commit forms, so a refusal — a detached HEAD, an ambiguous trunk — leaves the working copy exactly as it was: parked on a non-trunk bookmark ship appends to it and names it in the report, on trunk it appends in your own repositories and starts a branch named from the commit subject when GitHub says the repository is someone else's, and `--branch <name>` (jj alias `--bookmark`) or `--new-branch[=<name>]` targets a different branch explicitly. Ship also refuses an empty working copy (`nothing to commit — did a prior ship already land <sha>?`), so a double-run cuts no empty duplicate — a no-diff merge or a conflicted `@` still commits. Drop to the manual `jj` steps when ship still doesn't fit, like a multi-commit split. An updated remote is not one of those cases: ship fetches first and rebases the stack onto the target itself — on plain-git repos too, autostashing uncommitted work — rolling back and reporting a rebase that would conflict, and a push rejected because origin advanced again mid-ship re-fetches, re-rebases, and retries (up to 3 attempts) before failing with the manual steps. A rejected `--amend` push is the exception: ship refuses rather than force-retrying over the concurrent push. The manual recovery — `jj git fetch` then `jj rebase` (your in-flight `@` rides along untouched) — remains for non-ship flows and for resolving a conflicted rebase ship refused; never `git stash` or a worktree + cherry-pick dance.

**Watch CI after every push.** A push that kicks off CI isn't done until every run is green. `ccx vcs ship` folds this in — it pushes, then watches every workflow run on the pushed commit (found by `--commit`, retrying registration for up to a minute) and reports each run's conclusion, duration, and URL, plus failing jobs and a `--budget`-capped log excerpt when a run goes red; on a terminal the watch streams live. A `CI error` segment means the watch itself hit an infra failure after a successful push — the report's `check:` line says how to resume; a bare re-run of ship refuses (nothing to commit) instead of cutting a duplicate. For a push ship didn't make, watch the run to completion yourself before you stop — `gh run watch "$(gh run list -L1 --json databaseId -q '.[0].databaseId')" --exit-status` — and never walk away from a red run: when the failures are mechanical (lint, format, vet — pre-existing baseline debt included), fix them forward in an immediate follow-up commit; report-only (a cc-notes bug) is reserved for failures that need a design or owner decision. (`--exit-status` exits non-zero when the run fails; give the run a moment to register before watching.)

Stack provider selection prefers native GitHub stacks (`<git-common-dir>/gh-stack`, schema version 1, backed by the GitHub stack API) for new stacks while retaining the Graphite backend: actual native branch membership takes precedence, existing Graphite branch membership stays on Graphite until deliberately migrated, and `ccx.stack` (`github` or `graphite`) chooses the backend for new or untracked stacks (`--no-stack` bypasses both; `--no-gt` remains for legacy compatibility). Queue provider selection is configured separately via `ccx.queue` (such as `trunk`, authenticated with the scoped v2 `TRUNK_MERGE_API_KEY`) without assuming every native GitHub stack uses Trunk. In a repo riding the Graphite lane (`.git/.graphite_repo_config`, found through the git common dir in a linked worktree too), ship is gated before any mutation: `ccx.nogt` set in git config, GitHub saying the repo is someone else's, or Graphite reporting it cannot submit here each demote to the jj/git flow with the reason in a leading `lane <kind> (<reason>)` segment, and `ccx vcs info` (alias `lane`) reports the selected provider, verdict, and why without mutating anything. On the native GitHub stack lane or the gt lane, ship cuts or updates the stacked branch and lands it as a submitted PR (`--tip-only` preserves already-approved or queued lower commits) — published by default, `--draft` opts out — never committing onto trunk. `ccx vcs stack restack` is the one-command catch-up with trunk — `ccx vcs stack rebase --no-push` on a stack lane / jj fetch + rebase onto `trunk()` / git replay onto the fetched remote trunk — and a conflict stops in a `conflict-<branch>` workspace, where `ccx vcs stack continue` finishes and `ccx vcs stack abort` drops the run; `ccx vcs stack submit` restacks and resubmits the whole stack; and the signal needn't stop at CI: `ship --reviews` keeps streaming review comments until the submitted PRs merge or close, and `ccx vcs reviews` attaches the same watch to an existing PR.

**Releases.** Tagging `v*` triggers `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which runs goreleaser to build the binaries, cut a GitHub release, and push the Homebrew cask to `yasyf/homebrew-tap`. The version comes from the tag. The release refuses to run unless the tagged commit is on `main` — tag a merged commit (e.g. `git tag vX.Y.Z origin/main`), not a feature branch. One-time setup requires `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` plus all five `MACOS_*` repository secrets. Darwin artifacts are Developer-ID-signed and notarized; missing credentials fail the release before publication (see `reference/go-ci-and-release.md`).
